headline: Europe Opens the Compute Tender
deck: Europe has invited bids for up to seven AI gigafactories, with awards due in early 2027 and operations targeted within 18 months of signature. The €30 billion headline remains a funding target whose chips, grid works, sites and private capital still have to be assembled.
body: On 30 July, the Union moved the AI-gigafactory program into an open call for tenders covering up to seven projects, with bids due on 12 November 2026. [E1][E2] Evaluation is assigned to the EuroHPC Joint Undertaking, award decisions are expected by early 2027, and framework plus specific contracts are then meant to permit construction to start during 2027. [E2] Selected facilities are expected to begin operating within a maximum of 18 months from signature, creating distinct gates for bid, award, contract, construction, installation and live service. [E2] At publication, the releases disclosed no winning site, signed accelerator order, grid connection agreement, committed private financing or commissioned capacity; those remain proposal inputs and later delivery obligations. [E1][E2]

The capital stack starts with up to €10 billion in EU and national support and an expectation of at least €20 billion in private investment. [E1][E2] Lot 1 can support four projects with up to €100 million of EU funding in phase one and another €400 million in phase two, producing a maximum EU envelope of €2 billion if every slot reaches both phases. [E2] Lot 2 can support three projects with up to €200 million in phase one and another €800 million in phase two, producing another €3 billion EU ceiling. [E2] Participating states are to match EU funding, so the published arithmetic reaches €5 billion from the Union, as much as €5 billion nationally and an expected €20 billion privately; the €30 billion headline is a target capital stack with expenditure still ahead. [E1][E2]

Capability is specified through multiples of the processor count in Europe’s most powerful existing AI factory. [E2] Each Lot 1 project must begin with at least that baseline and rise to at least three times it in phase two, while Lot 2 is framed at up to twice the baseline initially and at least four times it in phase two. [E2] The releases provide no absolute accelerator count, model mix, memory configuration, interconnect design or delivered-training benchmark, leaving the commercial bids to translate processor ratios into usable capacity. [E1][E2] Processor count therefore acts as an entry threshold; rack density, network fabric, software efficiency, power draw and availability will determine how much productive compute buyers receive from the installed fleet. [E1][E2]

Eighteen states signed the joint procurement agreement with EuroHPC JU: Croatia, Czechia, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Ireland, Italy, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Portugal, Slovakia, Spain and Sweden. [E2] Consortia or special-purpose vehicles may apply by combining companies, public bodies, investors and other partners, and a project may sit in one state, span several locations or use a cross-border distributed design. [E2] EuroHPC JU and those states intend to procure compute-access time from successful facilities, giving the public side a customer role alongside its financing role. [E2] Sovereignty is presently expressed through European deployment, compliance with EU rules, public access procurement and permission to source hardware from Europe or like-minded countries; the releases provide no formula for equity ownership, board control, operator control or investor exit. [E1][E2]

Hardware access remains an upstream dependency. [E2] The Commission says it signed letters of intent with AMD, Nvidia and Qualcomm to support seamless access to necessary hardware following the EU-US trade deal. [E2] Those letters disclose no processor model, quantity, price, delivery window, export authorization or reserved production slot in the two releases, while consortia remain free to procure from providers in Europe or like-minded countries during either development phase. [E2] The accelerator gate closes only when a selected consortium converts supplier interest into binding purchase terms, delivery schedules, financing and acceptance tests tied to the facility build. [E1][E2]

The procurement is structured around compute-access time, yet the asset behind that service must combine advanced processors, software and cloud stacks, high-speed connectivity and an energy-efficient data centre. [E1][E2] That design channels capital through a consortium or special-purpose vehicle into chips, racks, networking, buildings, power conversion, cooling equipment, land and civil works before public buyers can consume the contracted access. [E1][E2] A credible 18-month plan must align land control, permits, utility studies, grid connection, substations, transformers, cooling-water or closed-loop cooling design, construction sequencing, operator staffing and commissioning. [E1][E2] The operating clock is therefore an integrated delivery test: a late permit, transformer, grid bay, cooling system or software acceptance milestone can strand completed equipment while financing costs continue. [E1][E2]

The strongest counter-case to the €30 billion headline is the program’s own arithmetic and sequence: a maximum €5 billion EU envelope, matched national funding and an expected €20 billion private contribution remain conditional on acceptable bids, awards and later contracts. [E1][E2] An open tender can expose whether sponsors possess credible sites, utilities, suppliers, operators and equity, while the tender itself supplies none of those physical inputs. [E1][E2] Competition may still reduce uncertainty by forcing each consortium to price dependencies, assign risk and commit to a schedule that can be evaluated before public access is purchased. [E2] The hardest gate is electricity delivery: accelerators can arrive at a warehouse, while a live high-capacity connection, substation, transformer train and cooling plant must exist at the chosen site before the machines can enter service. [E1][E2]

evidence_box.fragment: EU launches AI Gigafactories call to boost Europe's computing capacity and unlock more than €30 billion in investment

evidence_box.fragment: Selected AI Gigafactories are expected to begin operations within a maximum of 18 months from the signature.

art.caption: Seven proposed gigafactories now have to disclose the chips, power, water and capital behind the promise.
